studies.name: AttendEase
studies.title: Giving back teachers their time through automated attendance
studies.summary: Manual roll call takes 5–7 minutes per class and still leaves room for error. AttendEase automates attendance, saving teachers time and providing accurate, real time data. I designed the brand and teacher/admin dashboards, collaborated with developers to launch a classroom pilot, and refined the experience using teacher feedback.

sections.title: Attendance processes create stress for teachers and school admins
sections.body:
Taking attendance sounds easy. But it’s manual, it’s repetitive, and when something inevitably goes wrong, everyone feels it: teachers, office staff, parents. Here’s what we kept hearing.

Before we brainstormed solutions, we went to schools. We interviewed teachers, sat in classrooms, and talked to the people who actually deal with attendance every day.

The interviews below are a snapshot of what insights we gathered to help shape a solution via an iOT device.

So how did we come to our solution, anyway?

sections.title: iOT device + a simple teacher app = AttendEase
sections.body:
What if attendance just… took itself?

AttendEase uses a small classroom camera to recognize students the moment they walk in. By the time the bell rings, attendance is already done.

The split view lets teachers immediately focus on who’s missing. It follows the F-shaped reading pattern: absent students on the left where the eye naturally goes first, since those are the ones requiring teacher action.

Teachers and admins have completely different jobs, so they needed completely different dashboards. Admins aren’t taking attendance, they’re watching patterns. So their view is built around trends over time, grade-level data, and a flag for students who might be chronically skipping. Principals pretty much said the same thing: they care most about accurate reporting for funding sake and seeing things get better over time.

AttendEase classroom camera and teacher dashboard

Selected AttendEase dashboard design with separate absent and present student lists

AttendEase administrator dashboard with school-wide attendance overview

First iteration, designed to answer school-wide questions, not individual classroom ones

sections.title: iOT device + a simple teacher app = AttendEase
The original MVP
sections.body:
We explored a few potential solutions — RFID being the obvious one. Talking to schools, we found that some were already experimenting with it: tags on backpacks, cards students scan at the door. It sounds simple. But the issues became clear fast.

Any solution that requires a student to remember something, carry something, or do something wasn’t foolproof. Forgotten tags, kids who just don’t scan — these techniques weren’t solving the problem, just moving it.

Facial recognition worked because it asked nothing of the student. They walk in. That’s it. That’s the whole interaction.

Why we built a standalone MVP: the chicken-and-egg problem

We never wanted AttendEase to be its own platform. The real vision is a lightweight integration that lives inside Infinite Campus or PowerSchool, so teachers never have to learn anything new.

But when we reached out to those companies — we actually got on a Zoom with PowerSchool — we hit a wall. They wouldn’t integrate with us until we were already in schools. And schools didn’t want us until we had that integration.

So the standalone MVP was a deliberate wedge. Build just enough to run a real pilot, get real data, and go back to the SIS platforms with actual proof.

Design → AI code → redesign

To move faster, our developer used AI to code the initial dashboard, but the result looked noticeably different from my Figma designs, sort of keeping the branding but a little off..

Rather than nit picking the pixel differences for our pilot stage, I developed a rapid iteration workflow: I take screenshots of the coded output on our live dashboard pilot website, bring them into Figma, iterate directly on top of them, and feed those updated designs back into the AI for the next build cycle.

This let me stay in Figma (where I’m fastest) while still directly shaping the coded product. It also meant I could evaluate AI’s design decisions alongside my own. It wasn’t my ideal dashboard, but once connected to the dashboard it made a great prototype.

With our pilot dashboard in place, I decided my next step would be figuring out which variations of the attendance data visualization would be best. I answered that question by taking the designs to 10 real teachers for testing. Each version below shows what I changed, why, and the results of those tests.

sections.title: The original MVP
How do you make an ed-tech brand feel trustworthy?
sections.body:
Facial recognition in schools comes with a lot of questions, and rightfully so. Our design needed to answer those questions through the branding — feel safe and professional, but easy.

I built AttendEase’s visual identity around those values.

To start the UI design process, I built a design system in Figma to keep everything consistent as I designed.

I built four variable collections in Figma: Alias, Brand, Mapped, and Responsive, totaling 98 alias tokens and 51 mapped tokens. Semantic names like action, present, and error kept the UI consistent and made light/dark mode a single swap.

The logo colors were the basis for the system and doubled as state indicator colors for the attendance UI pretty well.

Poppins’ rounded letterforms create a friendly tone that felt right for a product used by teachers daily. I paired it with Inter for body text and data-heavy screens.

sections.title: How do you make an ed-tech brand feel trustworthy?
A 2 week-long pilot proved the tech and saved teachers ~34 minutes a day
sections.body:
We made a connection with the head of technology at American Heritage Schools who allowed us the opportunity to pilot in a real classroom environment. Our goals were to validate both the facial recognition hardware and the teacher dashboard experience under actual conditions. The pilot results discovered that our system cut attendance time from 5–7 minutes to under 45 seconds per period.

Testing our MVP at American Heritage Schools

We worked with the school’s IT team to install the camera. We also worked with the school to send out permission slips to parents for the students to participate in the test. As they installed the camera, I ran user tests on Mr. Hancock and observed how he interacted with the dashboard and what his preferences were.

After the trust-building curve in week one, teachers reduced attendance time from a 5–10 minute manual process to a 30–45 second review-and-submit. Across 5 class periods, that’s roughly 34 minutes returned to instruction every day, or over 100 hours per teacher per school year.

Testing our camera in a BYU Lecture Hall

We took our camera into a massive BYU lecture hall to see if our tech could actually handle a crowd of 100 students. To keep ourselves honest, we had every student fill out a Google Form with their section via a map I made so we could compare our camera’s “vision” against where people were actually sitting. The professors cooperated with us to provide the students’ ID pictures for testing purposes.

For the first 25 minutes, everything worked. The camera picked out faces in a sea of 100 students, matching them to sections in real time. We were watching the detection data come in live and it felt amazing to see what it was capable of.

Then we were met with a little trouble when someone accidentally kicked the power strip and the camera lost power halfway through the lecture. Sadly all of our data was gone.

That moment exposed a critical gap: we had no local data buffer. If the connection drops, even for a second, everything captured up to that point disappears. Our developer immediately prioritized building a local fail-safe so the system saves detection data continuously, independent of the power or network state. Without that failure, we would have shipped a product that silently loses data any time something goes wrong.

AttendEase has completed two competitive funding rounds through BYU’s Rollins Center for Entrepreneurship & Technology, presenting to judges and reporting on progress milestones each round. Total funding to date: $5,000.

Two charter school expos, 50+ educator conversations, and a shifted pitch

We exhibited at two private school and charter school tradeshows: one in Las Vegas and one in Utah. As the sole designer, my role expanded to “tradeshow booth designer”. I designed all the marketing and promo materials, mapped out the booth layout to scale, and then actually built it: laser cutting and painting our wood signage (color matching our exact brand orange with paint chips on the Home Depot floor). It would be our first time in front of potential adopters for our pilot program which meant we needed to show up looking like a real product, not a class project.

studies.name: Lucid Internship
studies.title: UX design internship at Lucid Software
studies.summary: Product design work from my summer internship at Lucid Software, the company behind Lucidchart and Lucidspark.

sections.title: A summer of product design at Lucid Software
sections.body:
During my summer internship at Lucid Software, the company behind Lucidchart and Lucidspark, I worked on enterprise monetization, user activation, and licensing alongside senior product managers, staff engineers, and UX researchers.

Most of my time went into finding friction in how people move between access levels, auditing high-volume conversion funnels, and testing design ideas through quick internal research. Each project below is a different problem I worked on during the internship.

sections.title: What I took away from enterprise UX at this scale
sections.body:
• The biggest breakthrough came from stepping back to audit how the system actually behaved before jumping into high-fidelity design, so I learned to question the brief early.
• Working closely with engineering, product management, and QA kept our decisions grounded in what was technically possible and caught edge cases early.
• In enterprise software, clear feedback and trust matter far more than growth prompts or pushy funnels.

studies.name: Reviive
studies.title: Turning costly product returns into community donations
studies.summary: I designed Reviive from 0→1, a platform that catches low-value product returns before they’re liquidated or landfilled and routes them to nearby nonprofits instead. I did the branding, the product design, and the dashboard nonprofit volunteers use.

sections.title: What Reviive does
sections.body:
When a customer returns a product, the company ships it to a warehouse, inspects it, and works out whether the resale value justifies the processing cost. For low-value items it usually doesn’t, so those returns get bulked together and liquidated, destroyed, or sent straight to a landfill.

Reviive intercepts that flow. Companies flag items as eligible for donation, and Reviive automatically routes those returns to a nearby nonprofit. A volunteer scans the item using the Reviive Dashboard, the customer gets their refund, and the item is logged in the nonprofit’s inventory, ready to go to community members who need it.

Companies save on processing costs and get a tax deduction, less ends up in landfills, and the goods reach families who can use them.

sections.title: Understanding where returned goods end up
sections.body:
Research · $817B in annual returns, and 8.4 billion pounds of usable goods landfilled every year

Before designing anything, I needed to understand the full ecosystem. Retail returns cost companies $817 billion a year (NRF, 2024), 44% of returned items are never resold (EU study, 2021), and the process creates an estimated 15 million tons of CO₂ emissions (Retail Dive). That’s 8.4 billion pounds of usable goods landfilled every year while families in need go without basic necessities.

Team sprint · From an assigned prompt to a shared idea in four weeks

Reviive started as a team project. For the first half, I worked with three teammates to explore the returns problem space, map stakeholders, and settle on the concept. Then I took it on solo for branding, design, prototyping, and testing.

The problem we set out to tackle was how to reduce returns waste and save retailers money.

Stakeholders · Three groups with one thing in common

I mapped three core stakeholders: retailers buried in processing costs, nonprofits facing surging demand with limited inventory, and communities that can’t access the goods being destroyed. Each group had its own pain points, but the current system wastes resources because nothing lines up the needs of all three.

Persona · Designing for Lindsey

From there, I built a primary persona: Lindsey Right, a 49-year-old Donations and Outreach Coordinator at a nonprofit in Austin. She’s passionate about impact but overwhelmed by manual processes like spreadsheets, emails, and hand-sorting, and she isn’t very tech-savvy. Designing for Lindsey meant the dashboard had to be simple, scannable, and built around tasks rather than data.

sections.title: Research
Team sprint
Designing a dashboard volunteers can use without training
sections.body:
The core interaction · Scan the item, and the dashboard logs everything else

A volunteer at a nonprofit receives a routed return, opens the Reviive Dashboard, and scans the item. The system logs it into inventory with the item details, condition, and donor information, so nobody has to enter data by hand.

Wireframes · Starting with the screen volunteers use most

I started wireframing the Returns Management page, where volunteers spend most of their time. V1 used a traditional spreadsheet table separating incoming and processed returns, but testing showed volunteers struggled to scan rows quickly. V2 replaced rows with visual cards showing item photos and added filter chips for time and region. The detail modal, which opens when a package is scanned, lists every item inside with its size, category, and a one-tap status action.

The Inventory Management and Distribution pages went through a similar process. For inventory, volunteers needed to see all available stock at a glance, check item details, and add donations by hand. For distribution, the challenge was creating orders across several clothing categories for families while managing community member profiles and a cart. I explored several interaction patterns for each.

sections.title: Wireframes
Designing for volunteers with little to no training
sections.body:
I wanted Reviive to feel fresh but simple. I stayed away from harsh blacks and whites and stuck with soft dark greens and pale yellows to create a gentler, friendlier feel.

Components · Inspired by inventory tools, adapted for volunteers

I took inspiration from inventory systems like Shopify and ReturnGo, but adapted them for volunteers instead of professional staff. Everything came back to my persona: charity workers don’t have time to learn fancy new software.

I also added small motivational touches, like the daily progress bar and hover animations, to give volunteers a little hit of satisfaction when they finish a task, which matters when the work can feel repetitive. I wanted something intuitive and even a little fun to use that mostly stays out of the way.

sections.title: Designing for volunteers with little to no training
Testing revealed gaps in sorting, messaging, and scan feedback
sections.body:
High-fidelity prototype · Testing the returns page first

For this sprint, I focused on redesigning and testing the returns management (Donations) page. The flow walks through the key states a volunteer runs into: connecting the scanner, scanning a package, reviewing each item inside, and seeing the table update after processing. Click any screen to enlarge it and step through the flow.

User flow · Answering the questions that came up in testing

To improve the first prototype, I made a more complete flow that answered the questions volunteers asked during testing, and I tweaked the messaging to make managing donations clearer. That meant UI and UX changes to the prototype.

• What do I do if my scanner isn’t connecting?
• Is there a way to enter the item manually?

V2 prototype · Progress bars, manual entry, and multi-item animations

After working in all the testing feedback and the new user flow, I built the final V2. It adds a progress bar for the day, manual entry and scanner troubleshooting flows, interactive hover states, and animations for packages with several items.

sections.title: What I learned and what I’d do with more time
sections.body:
Designing Reviive from 0 to 1 for three different groups (retailers, nonprofits, and the people receiving donations) taught me how much it matters to design for non-technical users who are working in a fast-paced setting.

If I had more time · Three things I’d build next

• Field test with nonprofit volunteers during peak donation intake, to refine how scanning feels and what happens when the scanner can’t read a label.
• Build a dashboard for retailers with automatic tax receipts and live carbon-offset numbers for their sustainability reporting.
• Prototype accessible mobile notifications for community members receiving high-demand donated items.

studies.name: Barkcelona
studies.title: A soccer ball dog toy built for dogs, not just their owners
studies.summary: A consumer research project about what makes a dog toy engaging, durable, and worth buying. We walked the dog toy aisle at Walmart, interviewed seven dog owners, and ended up designing Barkcelona, a solid rubber soccer ball with hollow treat pockets and a parody FC Barcelona brand.

sections.title: What Barkcelona is
sections.body:
Barkcelona is a soccer ball dog toy made of solid rubber, with hollow pockets you can fill with treats. It started as a consumer research project, where my team and I set out to understand what makes a dog toy engaging, durable, and worth buying.

We walked the dog toy aisle at Walmart, interviewed seven dog owners, and studied the best-selling toys online. The most popular soccer ball toy on Amazon turned out to fall apart within days, sometimes into pieces small enough to swallow. Barkcelona keeps what people love about that toy and fixes what makes it unsafe.

sections.title: Understanding what dogs and their owners want from a toy
sections.body:
Field research · Walking the dog toy aisle at Walmart

We started at a local Walmart to see what was on the shelf and how toys were grouped, priced, and marketed to owners. Almost everything was sold on the idea that pets are part of the family, so owners look for toys that are enriching, safe, and satisfying rather than cheap and disposable.

Interviews · What seven dog owners told us

We talked to seven owners whose dogs ranged from a young beagle mix to an older Labrador who didn’t care much for toys. A few things kept coming up. Dogs destroy plush toys quickly and the pieces can become a choking hazard, scent and treats keep a dog interested longer, and a good grip point makes a toy easier to pick up and shake.

Competitive analysis · Who each toy on the market is really designed for

We mapped existing toys by whether they get a dog moving or keep it busy, and by whether they’re designed around the dog or the owner. A lot of popular toys sit on the owner’s side. They’re funny or high tech, and the dog just goes along with them.

Benchmark · Reading the reviews of the top dog toy on Amazon

The QDAN soccer ball has 12,351 ratings and a 4.3 star average, but the reviews tell a different story. People loved the idea, and then their dogs tore off the nylon handles, popped the ball, and chewed it to pieces, sometimes within the first hour.

Problem · A durability and safety problem hiding inside a bestseller

The soccer ball is one of the most popular dog toy formats right now, and also one of the most dangerous. Its inflatable build tears, pops, and shreds into pieces small enough to swallow. Owners rank swallowing foreign objects as their top health concern for their pets, and about 15% of dog owners have watched their dog choke on a toy or a piece of one.

sections.title: Keeping the soccer ball and fixing what made it unsafe
sections.body:
Design direction · Designing for the dog and the owner at the same time

Owners want the fun of watching their dog chase a soccer ball, and they want the photo. What they don’t want is a trip to the vet because the toy shredded. The toy has to appeal to the person buying it off the shelf and to the dog, who cares about texture, scent, and how it feels to chew.

Design goals · Four goals that came from the gaps in the market

The toy needed to be durable enough for heavy chewers, entertaining enough to keep a dog playing, friendly to how dogs see and carry things, and still feel like a real game of soccer.

Final design · Barkcelona, a soccer ball built to survive a dog

Every part of the design traces back to the research. The color blocking comes from how dogs see color, the panel layout from soccer ball geometry, and the concave ridges are sized to an average dog’s snout. The treat holes make the ball fun to chase, and they’re also why the core can be hollow, which keeps the ball light enough to carry.

sections.title: Final design
Keeping the soccer ball and fixing what made it unsafe
How the design came together
sections.body:
Ideation · Building a soccer ball that can survive a dog

We started with three open sketch directions, then focused on one question: how do you build a soccer ball that a dog can’t destroy? The answer was layers. An outer shell of puncture-resistant rubber, a textured middle for grip, and a hollow center that keeps the weight down and can hold treats.

Treat pockets · Turning the pentagons into treat pockets

A standard soccer ball has 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. We explored using the pentagon panels as openings that drop kibble as the ball rolls. The hollow sockets also give a dog something to grip, deep enough to get a snout in and lift the ball, but not so deep that the rubber walls get thin and tear. Packed with peanut butter, the same pockets turn a fetch toy into a lick toy.

Key decision · Cutting the handle

In the reviews that mentioned damage, the fabric handles on the QDAN ball were where the tearing started, because they gave dogs an easy place to bite and pull. We cut the handle early, so the final ball is handle-free, smooth-edged, and solid enough for long chewing sessions. Removing it was the first structural improvement over the existing toys.

Color and brand · Blue and yellow led to Barkcelona

Dogs see blue and yellow most clearly, so the color study started there. Those colors also belong to two of the biggest soccer clubs in the world, which is how the toy became Barkcelona, a parody of FC Barcelona. The name says what the toy is and where the idea came from, and the crest keeps the club’s shield shape while swapping in a dog bone banner, a paw print, and a soccer ball.

Physical prototype · Carving a full-size prototype out of foam

The sketches and renders only went so far. I needed to hold the ball, feel the ridges, and check the proportions at real size, so I carved one out of foam by hand. I traced the panel geometry onto a foam sphere, outlined every ridge in red marker, carved the recesses and punched the treat holes, then sealed it with gesso and painted it in the Barkcelona colors. It was the hardest prototype I’ve ever made.

It confirmed that a ridge depth of about 8 to 10 mm felt substantial without being harsh, and that the treat holes took out enough of the core to make the ball noticeably lighter. It was easy to carry in a dog’s mouth but still heavy enough to roll predictably.

Google Trends showed two directions in what people search for. One is durable toys that keep a dog’s mind busy, not just its body. The other is novelty toys that reflect the owner’s own identity, like Harry Potter or Dunkin’ themed toys. Highlighted searches below are brands marketed around enrichment and interactive play.

That means the toy has to appeal to two audiences at once: the person who buys it based on how it looks on the shelf, and the dog, who plays with it based on instinct and texture.

What this means for the design
Red and orange toys look brownish to dogs, so they’re vivid to owners but not to dogs.
Blue and yellow are the colors dogs see most clearly.
Contrast matters more than hue, because dogs track motion by contrast.
Texture, scent, and sound engage dogs more than how a toy looks.
Automatic ball launchers, suction cup balls, and rolling robots. They’re high tech and save the owner effort, so the dog exercises but the owner barely takes part.
Flirt poles, herding balls, and tug toys. They tap into a dog’s instincts to fetch, herd, and hunt, and keep both the dog and the owner engaged.
Harry Potter plush, coffee cup toys, and funny squeakers. They’re fun for the owner, and the dog mostly just puts up with them.
Competitive map: active versus passive play, owner-centric versus dog-centric design
The QDAN dog soccer ball, a top seller on Amazon
The QDAN dog soccer ball. Many sellers list the identical product.
Amazon customer reviews for the QDAN dog soccer ball

People are wired to find human-like behavior in animals adorable, and it happens before we even think about it. A toy that makes a dog look like it’s playing soccer sets that off right at the moment someone is deciding what to buy. It’s a feeling on the owner’s side, so the best toys delight the owner visually and satisfy the dog physically.

Disney’s Air Bud movies are built on one idea, a dog playing human sports: volleyball, baseball, soccer, and basketball. Each sequel makes the same emotional bet, and it kept working. The tagline, “He’s got the Golden touch,” is about giving a dog human athletic talent, which is anthropomorphism used as marketing.

studies.name: Lucid Internship
studies.title: We were solving the wrong problem
studies.summary: The brief asked me to redesign an upgrade prompt, but auditing the real flow showed the friction was somewhere else, so I reframed the problem before designing any screens.

sections.title: What I was asked to design
sections.body:
I was asked to design a modal to invite users to request a paid license.

Limited Access (free) enterprise users could have a pre-purchased license waiting for them on their company's Lucid account. I was asked to make that more visible and encourage them to claim it.

Users don't know a license is available.

Show a modal prompting them to request it.

Making the license more visible will increase requests.

sections.title: Finding out the brief was solving the wrong problem
sections.body:
Based on the original brief, I explored several ways to tell Limited Access users that a license was available: a modal, welcome pop up, banner, and an edit to what Lucid calls a "license chip.

At this point, I was still designing around the assumption that users needed to actively request or claim the license.

Rapid prototyping concepts exploring modal, welcome pop-up, banner, and license chip

I went to Preprod to figure out how the design would fit into the current flow

That's when I learned something that changed the trajectory of this project. I had been operating on the assumption that the need for this modal was validated, but discovered that users on auto-grant accounts were already upgraded automatically through high-intent actions due to a recent update to admin settings.

But the interaction logic started to fall apart.

The modal used CTA language like "Request a license" giving users a choice to dismiss the prompt.

On auto-grant accounts, if a user dismissed the prompt and continued into the canvas, it'd still trigger the license automatically anyway because that's the setting their company account was on.

That meant the interface could imply that the user had declined or postponed the license, while the system granted it anyway.

That inconsistency made me stop working on the UI and test the assumption from the original project assignment I was given.

The user didn't need to request a license. They already had one.

On auto-grant accounts, I found that the assumptions behind the original concept could not all be true at once. If an eligible license was available, Lucid could already grant it automatically after certain user actions.

sections.title: Early exploration
Discovery
Testing the new question with 15 users
sections.body:
I put together a research plan and ran 15 user tests in three days to understand whether users noticed when their account access type changed, whether they understood what their new access meant and if it mattered to them.

participants did not notice the "License granted" growl.

This was my original hypothesis confirmed. The few participants who noticed it described it as easy to miss.

participants did not understand the term "edit access."

Terms such as "full access" and "edit access" were inconsistently used across product, creating confusion.

Users cared more about what they could do than what tier they were on.

Most participants expressed this sentiment. Many did not care whether they were on a "Standard," "Free," or "Suite" tier unless that status prevented them from doing something.

sections.title: Redesigning the moment access changes
sections.body:
I redesigned the modal to improve clarity and trust in the moment the account access changed.

to create an animated illustration of the lock unlocking — giving the modal a moment of delight that made the access grant feel tangible and rewarding rather than like a system event happening in the background.

Make sure they know what just happened

They were getting full access either way, so I didn’t want it to feel like something happened behind their back to improve trust.

Help them understand what that actually gives them

In order for the user and the admin paying for the seat the most value out of their paid seat, it's important that the user understand what the seat gives them the power to do.

Their company had already paid for the seat. I wanted it to feel like, "Oh nice, I have access now," not, "Wait… did I just buy something?"

Final design: Lucid modal reading 'Welcome, User! We saved you a seat.' with annotated design decisions

sections.title: Design direction
What changed because of it
sections.body:
The biggest outcome was changing the direction of the work.

I caught a gap during my own pre-prod walkthrough, tested the assumption with 15 users, and found the original modal was solving the wrong problem. That helped shift the work toward making auto-grant easier to understand. I also caught a license-chip timing bug and passed other issues to the right teams.

I learned to question the brief.

This project taught me to validate the problem before diving deep into a solution. I was operating under the assumption that each project brief given to me had been validated but testing proved otherwise. The modal made sense on paper, but once I traced the actual system behavior, the premise behind it no longer held.

The most useful thing I did was question the assignment, investigate the flow for myself thoroughly in preprod, validate the gap with users, and redirect the work toward a problem supported by evidence.

sections.title: Fixing a delay between getting a license and seeing it
sections.body:
While auditing the auto-grant flow, I found a timing gap between when the backend assigned a license and when the interface showed it. Users who triggered a full license waited several seconds before their in-app badge changed from “Limited Access” to “Full Access.”

Working with engineering and QA, I mapped the lifecycle state changes, defined immediate optimistic UI updates, and helped write QA edge-case scenarios so people weren’t left confused while they were in the middle of editing a canvas.

studies.title: A charming, space-saving kitchen product designed from research to CAD
studies.summary: A full design process project starting from user interviews in college apartments, through rapid sketch brainstorming, concept refinement, and final CAD modeling. The result is a collapsible dish rack in a pastel palette — designed to solve real storage and cleanliness frustrations in shared kitchens.

studies.name: Sack-Back Windsor Chair
studies.title: A 30-minute perspective sketch of an 18th-century classic
studies.summary: A timed sketching exercise studying the iconic Sack-Back Windsor Chair (c.1760s). Starting from the original design, I sketched a 30-minute perspective study in Nano Banana, then ran the sketch through AI to render a modern leather + metal reinterpretation.

studies.name: Tripolina Folding Chair
studies.title: Sketching a 19th-century folding chair from structure to skin
studies.summary: A timed sketching exercise studying the Tripolina Folding Chair (c.1885, Joseph Beverly Fenby). Starting from the original canvas-and-wood design, I produced a 30-minute Nano Banana perspective study, then rendered it in AI as a warm leather + walnut reinterpretation.
